keyframe_review.note: Wrong place. The Cliopatria shape (71 cells, 17,956 km2) lies mostly outside Berg: 25 cells in Thuringia, 20 in Hesse, 6 in Lower Saxony and only 15 in North Rhine-Westphalia, although the page's capital is Düsseldorf ('Hauptstadt war Düsseldorf'), at 6.8E in the west. The page gives the 1806 land as Berg with Cleves (ceded by Prussia 15 Feb 1806) and, with the Rhine Confederation Act, Deutz, Königswinter, Vilich, Siegen, Dillenburg, Hadamar, Horstmar, Bentheim-Steinfurt and Rheina-Wolbeck. The page gives no 1806 area.

ledger.note: 15 March 1806: Napoleon puts the Duchy of Berg under Joachim Murat. 'On 15 March 1806, the French emperor put Berg under the rule of his brother-in-law Joachim Murat'; infobox 'Established: 15 March 1806'. The de page: 'Am 15. März 1806 trat König Maximilian I. Joseph von Bayern sein Herzogtum Berg an Napoleon ab' and Murat took possession at Cologne on 19 March. The fr infobox gives 25 December 1805 for Murat's sovereignty. The Düsseldorf radius is the researcher's reading of the Duchy of Berg.

region.text: Berg proper around Düsseldorf: 'Berg' under Murat from 15 March 1806

ledger.note: March 1806: Cleves east of the Rhine joins Berg. 'including territories of the former Prussian Duchy of Cleves east of the Rhine river'; the de page: 'das am 15. Februar 1806 von Preußen abgetretenen Herzogtums Kleve', taken into possession by Murat on 19 March 1806 as Duke of Cleves and Berg.

ledger.note: 1806: the Nassau-Orange principalities of Siegen, Dillenburg and Hadamar join Berg in the south, with the Rhine Confederation Act (12 July 1806, CoR page; 'Mit Wirkung vom 1. August 1806' Berg claims sovereignty). The page gives the year, not the month, for the additions. The counterpart is the Nassau-Orange lands of the page ('nassau-oranischem Besitz'); the principality-of-nassau-orange-fulda dossier (another batch) records the loss of 12 July 1806.

region.text: 'die aus nassau-oranischem Besitz stammenden Fürstentümer Siegen, Dillenburg und Hadamar'

ledger.note: 1806: the Rhine Confederation Act adds mediatised lands. The de page lists 'Deutz, Königswinter, Vilich, Siegen, Dillenburg, Hadamar, Horstmar, Bentheim-Steinfurt, Rheina-Wolbeck'. The fr page places Rheina-Wolbeck and Salm-Horstmar among the post-Tilsit Prussian-Rhineland additions, so the date of the northern lands is uncertain between 1806 and 1807.

ledger.note: 1807: after the Peace of Tilsit Berg receives Prussian lands. 'wurde nach der Niederlage Preußens bei Jena und Auerstedt (14. Oktober 1806) und dem Frieden von Tilsit erneut erweitert'; 'Bis zum Januar 1808 kamen ... meist ehemals preußische Gebiete hinzu' (Elten, Essen, Werden, Mark, Dortmund). The Tilsit page gives the Prussian treaty as signed 9 July 1807 and tabulates 'County of Mark, with Essen, Werden, and Lippstadt' among the ceded lands (it does not name Berg). The page gives no month and no per-territory year.

ledger.note: 1807: the Münster lands join Berg. The de page lists Münster, Tecklenburg and Lingen among the former Prussian lands added 'bis zum Januar 1808'; the en page says the lands were 'further enlarged by the annexation of the County of Mark, the Prince-Bishopric of Münster' plus Dortmund and minor territories. The fr page lists Münster, Tecklenburg, Rheda and Lingen after Tilsit. Year inferred from the Peace of Tilsit (1807); the page gives no month.

ledger.note: January 1808: France takes Wesel. 'Die Stadt Wesel wurde dagegen im Januar 1808 Teil Frankreichs'; the fr page: 'Wesel was ceded to France in 1808'.

13 December 1810: France annexes the northern Berg lands. The French Senate decided 'die Annexion der klevischen und bergischen Gebiete nördlich einer Linie von der Lippe über Haltern' (via Telgte to Borgholzhausen) into the new departments Ober-Ems and Lippe; the Ems department 'wurde 1811 von Frankreich annektiert'. The fr page puts the annexation of Ems-Supérieur in 1811 and gives no Senate date. The land passes to France from 1811, the year the Cliopatria shape changes.

union.text: Horstmar, Bentheim-Steinfurt and Rheina-Wolbeck north of Münster

region.text: the northern Berg lands, north of the line from the Lippe via Haltern and Telgte to Borgholzhausen (Ems department)

ledger.note: November 1813: after Leipzig the grand duchy collapses. 'Am 10. November 1813 hielt ein Vortrupp der alliierten Armeen unter dem Kosaken-General Jussefowitsch Einzug in Düsseldorf'; the interim Generalgouvernement Berg followed (1813-1815). The en page: Berg's existence 'came to an end when the French forces pulled back'; the Confederation of the Rhine was dissolved on 4 November 1813 (CoR page). The Congress of Vienna Final Act, Article XXIV, gave most of the land to Prussia; Bentheim and Lingen went to Hanover.

wars.name: War of the Fourth Coalition
wars.outcome: Prussia defeated at Jena and Auerstedt (14 October 1806) and by the Treaty of Tilsit of 9 July 1807, which 'stripped the country of about half its territory'; the Prussian lands Mark, Münster, Essen, Werden, Lingen, Tecklenburg and Cleves east of the Rhine passed to French client states, among them Berg (de page).
wars.note: Berg's own part is a contingent of 5,000 men (CoR membership table); no Berg ground was fought over, so no zones.

wars.name: War of the Sixth Coalition
wars.outcome: The Battle of Leipzig (19 October 1813) breaks the Confederation of the Rhine, dissolved on 4 November 1813; Allied troops enter Düsseldorf on 10 November (de page) and Berg ends.
wars.note: The campaign in Berg itself (the 'Knüppelrussen' riots, fr page) is not dated, so no zone.

certainty.note: The state was assembled piecemeal from mediatised lands and Prussian cessions; the page says the north-eastern lands lay cut off from the rest of the state and were reachable only through Salm.
Four departments, 12 arrondissements and 78 cantons were fixed by the Burgos decree of 14 November 1808; the 1810 cut follows a line from the Lippe via Haltern and Telgte to Borgholzhausen.

notes: All eight Cliopatria shapes are marked wrong. The 1806-1810 shapes lie mostly in Hesse, Thuringia and Lower Saxony (a mix of other states' land), the 1811-1813 shape and the 1815-1827 shapes lie in Thuringia, and the 1814 shape (102,879 km2) covers France, Belgium and the Rhineland: none is Berg. Corrections are my radius readings of the places the pages name (the pages give no boundaries); areas by the gazetteer: about 14,000 km2 in 1806, 26,000 in 1807, 18,700 in 1811 against the infobox 17,300 for 1811. Pages that disagree: the fr infobox starts Murat's sovereignty on 25 December 1805, en and de on 15 March 1806; the fr page puts Rheina-Wolbeck and Salm-Horstmar after Tilsit, de among the 1806 Rhine Act additions; the fr page dates the Vienna disposal 1816, de 1815. Not settled within the five-page budget: the first-french-empire dossier cites the Duchy of Arenberg page for 'Berg annexed Recklinghausen' (1810), which I did not open; the exact date of each 1807 transfer (Treaty of Paris, 1807-08, not opened); Gummersbach and Friesenhagen added later (fr page, undated); the principality-of-nassau-orange-fulda dossier (another batch) cites a page for 'Dortmund went to the Grand Duchy of Berg on 1 March 1808' and for the Nassau territories going to Berg and Nassau on 12 July 1806, which I did not open: if right, Dortmund came in 1808 from Nassau-Orange-Fulda rather than in 1807 from Prussia; the interim Generalgouvernement Berg and the Generalgouvernement between Weser and Rhine (Münster) 1813-1815 need an occupation entry by the occupying power (Russia/Prussia). Place names not in the gazetteer: Wesel, Siegen, Dillenburg, Hadamar, Hamm, Tecklenburg, Lingen (drawn here as coordinates with the place named in 'text'). The fr page's 'Gouvernement général de Berg' and the end of the grand duchy are dated from the de page (10 November 1813).
